pos: v. (to make publicly known, proclaim; rendering Hebrew qara, shama, Greek kerusso)
etymology: From Latin publicare, to make public, from populus, the people. To publish is to put a thing before a whole people, not to print it.
biblical_def: Publish in the Authorized Version has nothing to do with printing; it means to proclaim so that a whole people hears. Moses opens his song with it: “Because I will publish the name of the LORD: ascribe ye greatness unto our God” (Deu 32:3) — the name published first, the ascription following. Nehemiah's revival works the same way: they “publish and proclaim in all their cities” the command to keep the feast (Neh 8:15). The word also carries a hard warning about what not to publish. David's lament over Saul begs restraint: “Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice” (2Sa 1:20) — and the Philistines had already done exactly the opposite, sending Saul's head round “to publish it in the house of their idols” (1Sa 31:9). The same act serves God's name or His enemies' triumph, and the difference is entirely in what is proclaimed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines publish as to discover to mankind, to make known to people in general, to divulge as a private transaction — and to proclaim, promulgate or make known a law or edict.
webster_full: PUB´LISH, v.t. To discover to mankind or to people in general what before was private or unknown; to divulge, as a private transaction.
2. To promulgate; to make known by posting, or by reading in a church; as, to publish banns of matrimony.
3. To make known by proclamation; to proclaim; as, to publish a law or an edict.
4. To send a book into the world; to offer to the public.
scriptures: Deu 32:3
Because I will publish the name of the LORD: ascribe ye greatness unto our God.
Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.
Neh 8:15

And that they should publish and proclaim in all their cities, and in Jerusalem, saying, Go forth unto the mount, and fetch olive branches, and pine branches, and myrtle branches, and palm branches, and branches of thick trees, to make booths, as it is written.
And they cut off his head, and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish it in the house of their idols, and among the people.
corruption_summary: A publishing age with no discrimination about what it publishes — every failure of a brother broadcast in the streets of Askelon — and a church that publishes everything except the name.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 1:20 has become almost unintelligible to an age in which everyone publishes. David has every political reason to broadcast Saul's death; the man hunted him for years, and his fall clears David's path to the throne. And David's instinct is to suppress the report, because the enemies of God would rejoice over it. The Christian question about any disclosure is therefore not merely whether it is true, but who rejoices when it is told. The daughters of the Philistines are always watching, and the church supplies them with material daily.

The corresponding failure is silence about the one thing commanded. Moses says I will publish the name of the LORD, and Nehemiah's reformation moves by public proclamation of what was written. A congregation with a large communications output and no proclamation of the name has inverted Deuteronomy 32:3. Publish the name; guard the brother's shame.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara (H7121), to call out, proclaim; shama (H8085) in the causative, to cause to hear; Greek kerusso (G2784), to herald — the New Testament's word for preaching.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call, cry out, proclaim; Moses publishing the name of the LORD (Deu 32:3).
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings, publish good news; the root behind how beautiful are the feet (Isa 52:7).
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, publish, preach; a herald does not compose his message, he carries it (2Ti 4:2).
usage: “I will publish the name of the LORD” — the name first, the ascription after.
“Publish it not in the streets of Askelon” — ask who rejoices when it is told.
“To publish it in the house of their idols” — the enemy publishes too.

pos: v. (to utter formally, to declare a verdict; rendering Hebrew bata, tame/taher in the causative, Greek apophthengomai)
etymology: From Latin pronuntiare, to announce publicly. In Leviticus the word is judicial: the priest does not cause the condition, he declares it.
biblical_def: Pronounce is one of the most doctrinally loaded verbs in the Old Testament, because of what the priest does in Leviticus 13. He examines the plague and then “pronounce[s] him unclean” (Lev 13:3) or “pronounce[s] him clean” (Lev 13:6). The priest does not heal the leper or infect him; he inspects and declares, and his declaration determines the man's standing in the camp. This is the exact grammar of justification: a forensic pronouncement about a person's status, made by one with authority to make it, on the basis of what is actually there. Leviticus even records the strange case where total coverage yields a clean verdict — “if the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean” (Lev 13:13) — the man who admits the disease entirely is the man declared clean. The word also warns about rash speech: whatever a man “shall pronounce with an oath” binds him even when forgotten (Lev 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pronounce as to speak, to utter articulately, and then as to utter formally, officially or solemnly — as to pronounce sentence or a decree.
webster_full: PRONOUNCE, v.t. To speak; to utter articulately.
2. To utter formally, officially or solemnly.
Sentence is pronounced by the judge.
3. To speak or utter rhetorically; to deliver; as, to pronounce an oration. 4. To declare or affirm.
scriptures: Lev 13:3

And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean.
Then the priest shall consider: and, behold, if the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean that hath the plague: it is all turned white: he is clean.
Lev 13:6

And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague be somewhat dark, and the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean.
Lev 5:4

Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these.
corruption_summary: Justification recast as a transformation God works inside a man rather than a verdict God pronounces over him — the Roman error the Reformation answered, and the priest of Leviticus 13 settles.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation controversy over justification turns on precisely this verb. Rome teaches an infused righteousness — God makes a man righteous and then accepts him. The Reformed position, following Paul, is that God pronounces the ungodly righteous on the ground of Christ's imputed obedience, and that the pronouncement is not a legal fiction but a true verdict about a real transfer. Leviticus 13 supplies the grammar in advance: the priest's word does not create the condition, and it absolutely determines the standing. Justification is a courtroom word, not a clinic word.

Leviticus 13:13 is the verse to press, because it is so counter-intuitive that it can only be deliberate. Partial leprosy leaves a man unclean; leprosy that has covered all his flesh yields the verdict clean. The man who can still point to healthy skin is shut up; the man wholly consumed by it is declared clean and sent home. That is total depravity and free justification pictured in a skin disease, and it is why the gospel is heard as good news only by those who have stopped negotiating about how much of them is still sound.
roots_summary: Hebrew tame (H2930) in the causative, to declare unclean, and taher (H2891), to declare clean — both used of the priest's verdict; bata (H981), to speak rashly.
roots_lines: Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or declare unclean; in Lev 13 the causative form is a verdict, not an infection.
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be or declare clean; the priest pronounces clean the man wholly covered (Lev 13:13).
Hebrew bata (H981) — to speak rashly, babble; the oath pronounced with the lips and forgotten, which still binds (Lev 5:4).
usage: “The priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean” — a verdict, not a cause.
“If the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean” — total admission, clean verdict.
“Whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath” — rash words still bind.

pos: v. (to charge with a fault, to convict; rendering Hebrew yakach, Greek elegcho)
etymology: From Latin reprobare, to disapprove, reject — the same root as reprobate. To reprove is to test a thing and find it wanting, then say so.
biblical_def: Reprove is to bring a fault home to a person, and Scripture treats it as an act of love rather than hostility. Abraham reproves Abimelech over a stolen well and the two make a covenant that same day (Gen 21:25) — reproof clearing the ground for peace rather than destroying it. The Chronicler records God Himself doing it on His people's behalf: “he reproved kings for their sakes” (1Ch 16:21). Job supplies the hard qualification that separates real reproof from mere argument: “How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?” (Job 6:25) — his friends had volume and had not touched him, because words only reprove when they are right. Job also warns the reprover that he is himself under scrutiny: “He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons” (Job 13:10). And Paul makes it a standing ministerial duty with a temperature attached: “reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reprove as to blame, to censure, to charge with a fault to the face — and notes the sense of convincing of a fault, or proving it upon a person.
webster_full: REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure.
I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices. Ps. l.
2. To charge with a fault to the face; to chide; to reprehend.
3. To blame for; with of; as, to reprove one of laziness. 4. To convince of a fault, or to make it manifest.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Job 6:25
How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?
And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away.
He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons.
corruption_summary: Reproof reclassified as judgment or harm, so that the loving act Scripture commands is now the one act a friend may not perform — and, on the other side, harshness excused as faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning ethic makes acceptance the whole of love, and on that account reproof is an injury by definition. Scripture holds the opposite: faithful are the wounds of a friend, and it is the enemy's kisses that are deceitful. A friendship in which nothing may be said is not deeper than one in which it may; it is shallower, because it has been purchased by an agreement to leave each other alone. Proverbs makes reception of reproof the plainest test of wisdom there is — a reproof enters further into a wise man than a hundred stripes into a fool.

But Job 6:25 must be allowed its full weight against the reprovers. Job's friends were doctrinally confident, verbally fluent, and wrong, and he asks the devastating question: what doth your arguing reprove? Reproof that is not right words reproves nothing, however forcefully delivered. And Paul's command sets the manner along with the duty — with all longsuffering and doctrine — which excludes both the silence that will not speak and the impatience that speaks without teaching.
roots_summary: Hebrew yakach (H3198), to decide, adjudge, reprove, correct — a legal root; Greek elegcho (G1651), to convict, expose, bring to light — the Spirit's own work in John 16:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to argue a case, adjudge, reprove; the same verb in come now, and let us reason together (Isa 1:18).
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, refute, expose; the Comforter shall reprove the world of sin (John 16:8), so reproof is a work of the Spirit before it is a duty of men.
Greek epitimao (G2008) — to rebuke, censure sharply; distinguished from elegcho, which aims at conviction rather than mere censure.
usage: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” — duty and manner together.
“What doth your arguing reprove?” — fluency is not the same as right words.
“He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons” — the reprover is watched too.

pos: n. and v. (a naming, a bringing to remembrance; rendering Hebrew zakar, Greek mneia)
etymology: From Latin mentio, a calling to mind, from mens, the mind. The Hebrew idiom is to make remembrance — naming a thing is bringing it into the mind.
biblical_def: Mention in Scripture is never casual, because to name a thing is to bring it into the mind and to give it standing. The law therefore governs it: “make no mention of the name of other gods, neither let it be heard out of thy mouth” (Exo 23:13), repeated by Joshua as a condition of survival in the land (Jos 23:7). The prohibition is not superstition; it is the recognition that habitual naming shapes affection. Positively, the psalmist confines his boasting to one subject: “I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only” (Psa 71:16). Isaiah makes it a missionary duty — “make mention that his name is exalted” (Isa 12:4). And Joseph supplies the poignant human case, asking the butler to “make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house” (Gen 40:14) — a request forgotten for two full years, until God's time made the mention effective.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mention as a hint, a suggestion, a brief notice or remark expressed in words or writing — and as a verb, to speak or write a brief notice of any thing.
webster_full: MEN´TION, n. A hint; a suggestion; a brief notice or remark expressed in words or writing; used chiefly after make.
Make no mention of other gods. Josh. xxiii.
MEN´TION, v.t. To speak; to name; to utter a brief remark; to state a particular fact, or to express it in writing.
I will mention the lovingkindnesses of the LORD. Is. lxiii.
scriptures: And in all things that I have said unto you be circumspect: and make no mention of the name of other gods, neither let it be heard out of thy mouth.
I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.
But think on me when it shall be well with thee, and shew kindness, I pray thee, unto me, and make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house:
Isa 12:4
And in that day shall ye say, Praise the LORD, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted.
corruption_summary: Speech treated as inert — mere words, naming nothing and forming no one — where Scripture governs what a covenant people may habitually name because naming shapes loving.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 23:13 offends the modern assumption that words are neutral containers. Why should God care whether a name is heard out of thy mouth? Because what a people constantly names, it eventually reverences. The prohibition is a discipline of the affections applied at the level of vocabulary, and it explains why Scripture is so attentive to speech habits generally. A Christian who has absorbed the culture's vocabulary about sex, success, or the self has already absorbed a good deal of its theology, whatever he professes.

The positive discipline is Psalm 71:16 — thy righteousness, even of thine only. The psalmist is not forbidden to speak of anything else; he is naming his one boast. And Genesis 40:14 gives the pastoral comfort for those who feel forgotten. Joseph asked to be mentioned, and was not, for two years. The mention came at the hour that put him before Pharaoh at the exact moment of the dream. Delay is not neglect when God governs the calendar.
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar (H2142), to remember, and in the causative to make mention, memorialize; Greek mneia (G3417), remembrance — Paul's making mention of you in my prayers.
roots_lines: Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, name, mention; the same root as zikkaron, a memorial, so mentioning is memorializing.
Greek mneia (G3417) — remembrance, mention; Paul's repeated without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers (Rom 1:9).
Greek mnemoneuo (G3421) — to call to mind, be mindful of; remember them that are in bonds (Heb 13:3).
usage: “Make no mention of the name of other gods” — what a people names, it comes to reverence.
“I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only” — one boast.
“Make mention of me unto Pharaoh” — forgotten two years, and then exactly on time.

pos: v. (to express gratitude; rendering Hebrew yadah, Greek eucharisteo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thancian, related to think — to thank is to think upon a benefit. The Hebrew yadah means to hold out the hands, so thanks is a posture before it is a sentence.
biblical_def: Thank is in Scripture an appointed office, not merely a mood. David “appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, and to record, and to thank and praise the LORD God of Israel” (1Ch 16:4), and set men “to stand every morning to thank and praise the LORD, and likewise at even” (1Ch 23:30) — thanksgiving on a rota, twice daily, whatever anyone felt. There were also thank offerings, brought by those “of a free heart” (2Ch 29:31), so the appointed and the spontaneous stood side by side. David's great prayer models the content: “Now therefore, our God, we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name” (1Ch 29:13) — offered while giving away a fortune, and thanking God for the ability to give it. Daniel thanks God in a death sentence (Dan 2:23), and the Lord Jesus thanks the Father for a doctrine hard to bear — that these things are hid from the wise and revealed unto babes (Mat 11:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thank as to express gratitude for a favor, to make acknowledgments to one for kindness bestowed — noting that the word is often used ironically.
webster_full: THANK, v.t. To express gratitude for a favor; to make acknowledgments to one for kindness bestowed.
We thank a man for his assistance.
We are bound to thank God always for you. 2 Thess. i.
THANK, n. Expression of gratitude; an acknowledgment made to express a sense of favor or kindness received.
scriptures: And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, and to record, and to thank and praise the LORD God of Israel:
Now therefore, our God, we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name.
Dan 2:23

I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast now made known unto us the king's matter.
At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
corruption_summary: Gratitude reduced to a wellness practice aimed at the self — thankfulness without a Person to thank — and, in the church, restricted to the occasions a man happens to feel it.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic version of gratitude is directed nowhere. It is recommended for its effects on the grateful — better sleep, better mood, better outlook — and its object is a vague abundance. Scripture's thanksgiving is transitive and personal: we thank thee. Strip out the Person and what remains is a technique, and a technique cannot survive a genuine calamity, because there is no one to thank when the harvest fails. Paul's in every thing give thanks (1Th 5:18) is only sane if Someone governs every thing.

The churchly failure is the opposite: waiting to feel thankful. David's Levites stood every morning and every evening by appointment, which means thanksgiving was rendered on days when no one was in the mood. That is not hypocrisy; it is the ordinary shape of covenant obedience, and feeling generally follows practice rather than preceding it. Daniel gives thanks under a decree of execution, and the Lord Jesus gives thanks for a hard doctrine of sovereign hiding and revealing — which is the highest reach of the word in Scripture.
roots_summary: Hebrew yadah (H3034), to hold out the hand, confess, give thanks — the same verb rendered confess; todah (H8426), a thank offering; Greek eucharisteo (G2168), to give thanks.
roots_lines: Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to throw out the hand, hence to confess or give thanks; confession of sin and thanksgiving are the same gesture in Hebrew.
Hebrew todah (H8426) — a thank offering, a confession; brought by those of a free heart (2Ch 29:31).
Greek eucharisteo (G2168) — to be thankful, give thanks; the root of eucharist, and the verb used of the Lord over the bread.
usage: “To thank and praise the LORD God of Israel” — thanksgiving as an appointed office.
“We thank thee, and praise thy glorious name” — said while giving a fortune away.
“I thank thee, O Father… because thou hast hid these things” — thanks for a hard doctrine.

pos: v. (to salute, to address with kindness on meeting; rendering Hebrew shaal le-shalom, Greek aspazomai)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon gretan, to approach, address. The Hebrew idiom is literally to ask after his peace — a greeting is an enquiry about another's welfare.
biblical_def: Greet looks like the least theological word in the New Testament and turns out to be one of the most instructive. Romans 16 is a whole chapter of greetings, and Paul names some twenty-six people individually: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” (Rom 16:3); “Greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us” (Rom 16:6); “Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord” (Rom 16:8). The apostle who wrote the deepest exposition of justification in the canon ends it by naming individual saints, several of them women, several of them slaves by their names, and remembering what each one did. Twice he commands the form: “Greet ye one another with an holy kiss” (1Co 16:20). And the Old Testament shows greeting as a mission: David sends ten young men to “greet him in my name” (1Sa 25:5), and Nabal's refusal of an ordinary courtesy nearly costs his whole household.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines greet as to address with expressions of kind wishes, to salute, to hail — and to congratulate, or to pay respects to at a distance by letter or message.
webster_full: GREET, v.t. To address with expressions of kind wishes; to salute; to hail; a term of civility.
2. To congratulate.
3. To pay compliments at a distance; to send kind wishes to.
GREET, v.i. To meet and salute. Salute one another; greet one another with a holy kiss.
scriptures: Rom 16:3
Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus:
Rom 16:6
Greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us.
All the brethren greet you. Greet ye one another with an holy kiss.
And David sent out ten young men, and David said unto the young men, Get you up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name:
corruption_summary: Christian fellowship reduced to attendance among strangers — a congregation of unnamed faces — where Paul closes his greatest epistle by naming saints one by one and remembering their labour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is practical, and Romans 16 measures it. Paul knew these people: which house the church met in, who had risked their necks, who had been in Christ before him, who had laboured much. A congregation where members can attend for years without being named, missed, or thanked is not simply less warm than the apostolic churches; it is structurally different from them, whatever its doctrine. Romans 16 is the last chapter of the Bible's greatest treatise on grace, and it is a list of names.

The principle to recover is that greeting is a covenant act, not a social lubricant. The Hebrew idiom asks after a man's shalom, and 1 Samuel 25 shows what refusing that costs: Nabal declines an ordinary courtesy to David's men and stands within hours of losing everything. Meanwhile Paul's holy kiss command should be felt even where the custom differs — the physical, unembarrassed warmth of it is the point, and a handshake offered as though to a stranger is not obviously its equivalent.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaal le-shalom, to ask after one's peace — the standard idiom for greeting; Greek aspazomai (G782), to enfold in the arms, salute, welcome — the word used twenty-one times in Romans 16.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, welfare; to greet is literally to ask after a man's peace (1Sa 25:5).
Greek aspazomai (G782) — to draw to oneself, embrace, salute; the verb that structures the whole of Romans 16.
Greek philema hagion (G5370, G40) — a holy kiss; commanded four times by Paul and once by Peter as a kiss of charity (1Pe 5:14).
usage: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” — named, and their labour remembered.
“Greet ye one another with an holy kiss” — commanded warmth, not mere civility.
“Go to Nabal, and greet him in my name” — and refusing it nearly cost a household.

pos: v. (to charge with a crime or fault; rendering Hebrew lashan, Aramaic akal qartsin, Greek kategoreo)
etymology: From Latin accusare, from ad causam, to call to account, to bring to the cause. An accusation is a formal summons to answer.
biblical_def: Accuse is a courtroom word that Scripture watches with suspicion, because of who does most of the accusing. Proverbs warns against it in ordinary life: “Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty” (Pro 30:10) — the accuser risks the guilt he tried to transfer. John the Baptist forbids it to soldiers with power to make it stick: “accuse any falsely” is set beside violence and extortion (Luk 3:14). The Gospels show accusation as the settled method of the Lord's enemies, who watch Him beside a man with a withered hand “that they might accuse him” (Mar 3:2) — a human being reduced to bait. And when the accusations finally come, “the chief priests accused him of many things: but he answered nothing” (Mar 15:3). Behind them all stands the original: Satan, “the accuser of our brethren… which accused them before our God day and night” (Rev 12:10), and the announcement that he is cast down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines accuse as to charge with, or declare to have committed a crime, either by plaint or complaint, information, indictment or impeachment — and to blame or charge with a fault.
webster_full: ACCUSE, v.t. To charge with, or declare to have committed a crime, either by plaint, or complaint, information, indictment, or impeachment.
2. To charge with a fault; to blame; to censure.
Their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another. Rom. ii.
It is followed by of before the subject of accusation.
scriptures: And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.
Mar 3:2
And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him.
Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty.
Luk 3:14
And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
corruption_summary: Accusation industrialized as a public form of entertainment and power, while the believer's standing answer to it — that the Accuser is cast down and an Advocate pleads — goes unused.
corruption_paragraphs: Public accusation is now a currency. It is cheap to make, expensive to answer, and rewarding to whoever makes it first, and Scripture's warnings read as if written for it. Proverbs 30:10 attaches a boomerang to the practice — the accuser is found guilty — and Mark 3:2 exposes the worst feature of accusation culture: the men watching Jesus were not interested in the man with the withered hand at all. He was an occasion. Whenever a real sufferer becomes useful chiefly as evidence against someone, Mark 3 is being re-enacted.

The pastoral half of this entry matters more. Many believers live under an accusing conscience that never rests, and Revelation 12:10 names the source: an accuser who works day and night. The answer is not to argue the charges, most of which are true, but to plead an Advocate. Christ answered nothing before the chief priests because He was accepting the charge on behalf of others. The accused Christian therefore has a defence he did not construct and cannot lose.
roots_summary: Hebrew lashan (H3960), to use the tongue, slander, accuse; Aramaic akal qartsin, literally to eat the pieces of a man — the idiom in Dan 3:8; Greek kategoreo (G2723), to speak against in court.
roots_lines: Hebrew lashan (H3960) — to slander with the tongue, accuse; the verb of Pro 30:10.
Aramaic akal qartsin — to eat the pieces of, a vivid idiom for malicious accusation; used of the Chaldeans who accused the Jews (Dan 3:8).
Greek kategoros (G2725) — an accuser, prosecutor; in Rev 12:10 it is the title of Satan, cast down.
usage: “The accuser of our brethren… which accused them before our God day and night” — and he is cast down.
“That they might accuse him” — a suffering man reduced to evidence.
“Accuse not a servant unto his master… and thou be found guilty” — the charge rebounds.

pos: v. (to own, confess, or recognize; rendering Hebrew yada, nakar, Greek homologeo, epiginosko)
etymology: From ac- (to) and knowledge — to bring a thing into the open as known. In Scripture acknowledgment is knowledge that has been owned, and owning it usually costs something.
biblical_def: Acknowledge is knowledge admitted aloud, and Scripture uses it for the two hardest admissions a man makes. The first is his own sin: “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid… and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Psa 32:5) — the acknowledging and the forgiving in one verse, with nothing between them. David repeats it in the great penitential psalm: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me” (Psa 51:3). Judah supplies the Old Testament's starkest instance, publicly owning both the pledge and the verdict: “Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I” (Gen 38:26). The second admission is God's right to direct a life: “In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths” (Pro 3:6) — not consult Him at the crossroads, but acknowledge Him in all the ways, which is why the promise of direction follows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acknowledge as to own, avow or admit to be true, by a declaration of assent — and to own or confess, as in relation to a fault or crime.
webster_full: ACKNOWL´EDGE, v.t. To own, avow or admit to be true, by a declaration of assent; as to acknowledge the being of a God.
2. To own or notice with particular regard.
In all thy ways acknowledge him. Prov. iii.
3. To own or confess, as in relation to a fault or crime. 4. To own with gratitude; as, to acknowledge a favor.
scriptures: Psa 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
Pro 3:6
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
And Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son. And he knew her again no more.
Psa 51:3
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
corruption_summary: Confession replaced by explanation — the account of oneself that acknowledges circumstances, upbringing, or misunderstanding, but never the sin — and guidance sought at crossroads by men who acknowledge God nowhere else.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern apology is a masterpiece of evasion: regret for how something was received, acknowledgment of impact, sorrow that offence was taken. Psalm 32:5 has a different grammar. I acknowledged my sin… mine iniquity have I not hid. The object of the verb is the sin itself, owned as the speaker's own, without a modifying clause. And the forgiveness follows immediately in the same sentence, which is the most encouraging thing about the verse — there is no waiting period between the honest admission and the pardon.

Proverbs 3:6 is the other correction, and it is routinely miscited. It is quoted as a decision-making formula: bring God the big choices and He will show you which way to go. But the text says in all thy ways, and the promise of direction is attached to that comprehensiveness. A man who acknowledges God in his work, his speech, his marriage, and his money is generally not agonizing over guidance, because the direction has been given continuously. Guidance is the fruit of an acknowledged Lordship, not a service offered to strangers.
roots_summary: Hebrew yada (H3045), to know, and in acknowledgment to know openly; nakar (H5234), to recognize, discern — Judah recognizing his own pledge; Greek homologeo (G3670), to say the same thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, acknowledge; the verb of Pro 3:6, knowing God in all one's ways.
Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to recognize, acknowledge; Judah acknowledging his signet, bracelets, and staff (Gen 38:26).
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to speak the same thing, agree, confess; confession is agreeing with God's verdict rather than offering one's own (1Jn 1:9).
usage: “I acknowledged my sin unto thee… and thou forgavest” — nothing stands between the two clauses.
“In all thy ways acknowledge him” — guidance is the fruit of comprehensive Lordship.
“She hath been more righteous than I” — Judah owns the pledge and the verdict together.

pos: interj. (an exclamation of grief, pity, or dread; rendering Hebrew ahah, oy, hoy)
etymology: From Old French a las, ah weary, from Latin lassus, weary. It is a word of exhaustion as much as of sorrow — the sound a man makes when he has no more argument left.
biblical_def: Alas is the Bible's cry of a man at the end of his resources, and Scripture records it without embarrassment on the lips of its best men. Aaron says it confessing sin: “Alas, my lord, I beseech thee, lay not the sin upon us” (Num 12:11). Joshua says it in something close to accusation after Ai: “Alas, O Lord GOD, wherefore hast thou at all brought this people over Jordan…?” (Jos 7:7) — a genuine complaint, and God answers not by rebuking the cry but by naming the sin in the camp. Gideon says it in terror at having seen the Angel of the LORD face to face (Jdg 6:22). Jephthah says it in the ruin of his own rash vow (Jdg 11:35). And the sons of the prophets say it over a borrowed axe head (2Ki 6:5) — which is worth noticing, because it shows the word is not reserved for catastrophe. Scripture leaves room for a man to cry out over a small disaster he cannot fix.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives alas as an exclamation expressive of sorrow, grief, pity, concern or apprehension of evil — and notes the phrase alas the day, and alas the while.
webster_full: ALAS´, exclam. An exclamation expressive of sorrow, grief, pity, concern, or apprehension of evil.
Alas the day! Alas the while! an exclamation of pity or regret.
Alas, my lord, how shall we do? 2 Kings vi.
Alas for the day! for the day of the LORD is at hand. Joel i.
scriptures: Jos 7:7

And Joshua said, Alas, O Lord GOD, wherefore hast thou at all brought this people over Jordan, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us? would to God we had been content, and dwelt on the other side Jordan!
And Aaron said unto Moses, Alas, my lord, I beseech thee, lay not the sin upon us, wherein we have done foolishly, and wherein we have sinned.
Jdg 6:22
And when Gideon perceived that he was an angel of the LORD, Gideon said, Alas, O Lord GOD! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face.
But as one was felling a beam, the axe head fell into the water: and he cried, and said, Alas, master! for it was borrowed.
corruption_summary: A piety that has no place for lament, so that grief and complaint are treated as failures of faith — where Scripture prints Joshua's alas and answers it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error is inside the church: a determined cheerfulness that regards lament as unbelief. But roughly a third of the Psalter is complaint, Lamentations is a canonical book, and Joshua 7:7 records Israel's greatest general asking God why He brought them over Jordan at all. God does not rebuke the question. He answers it — Israel hath sinned — and gives Joshua something to do. A faith with no alas in it has fewer resources than the Bible supplies, not more.

The principle to recover is that lament is addressed. Every alas in these passages is spoken to someone, mostly to the Lord GOD Himself, which is what separates biblical lament from despair and from grumbling. Despair speaks to no one; grumbling speaks to bystanders; lament speaks to God. And 2 Kings 6:5 keeps the category from becoming grand: a borrowed axe head in the Jordan is a small, humiliating trouble, and the prophet takes it seriously enough to act.
roots_summary: Hebrew ahah (H162), ah! alas! — a cry of distress, often opening a prayer; oy (H188) and hoy (H1945), woe — the prophets' word of impending judgment.
roots_lines: Hebrew ahah (H162) — alas, ah; Joshua's cry after Ai (Jos 7:7) and Gideon's at the Angel's appearing (Jdg 6:22).
Hebrew oy (H188) — woe, alas; a cry of pain over oneself, as Isaiah's woe is me (Isa 6:5).
Hebrew hoy (H1945) — ho! alas! woe! — the prophets' summoning cry, often opening an oracle of judgment (Isa 5:8).
usage: “Alas, O Lord GOD, wherefore hast thou at all brought this people over Jordan” — and God answers it.
“Alas, my lord… lay not the sin upon us” — the cry of confession.
“Alas, master! for it was borrowed” — a small, humiliating trouble taken seriously.

pos: adv. (with intensity and sincerity of purpose; rendering Hebrew intensive verb forms, Greek epagonizomai, ektenos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon eornost, zeal, seriousness. In the Authorized Version it usually renders a Hebrew doubled verb — protesting I protested, asking he asked — where intensity is built into the grammar.
biblical_def: Earnestly marks intensity of purpose, and the Authorized translators most often use it where Hebrew doubles a verb for emphasis. God says, “I earnestly protested unto your fathers… rising early and protesting, saying, Obey my voice” (Jer 11:7) — divine earnestness pictured as rising early, day after day, to say the same thing. The tenderest instance is God's word about a rebellious son: “since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him” (Jer 31:20) — the earnestness is God's memory of a child He has had to discipline. Job uses it of longing: a servant “earnestly desireth the shadow” (Job 7:2). Nehemiah applies it to bricklaying — Baruch “earnestly repaired the other piece” (Neh 3:20) — and Micah, chillingly, to sin: men “do evil with both hands earnestly” (Mic 7:3). Jude then makes it the church's duty toward doctrine: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines earnestly as warmly, zealously, importunately, eagerly, with real desire — and notes its use for intentness of purpose as well as intensity of feeling.
webster_full: EARN´ESTLY, adv. Warmly; zealously; importunately; eagerly; with real desire.
Being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly. Luke xxii.
2. With fixed attention; with eagerness.
3. With intentness of purpose or application.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.

Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD.
Jer 11:7
For I earnestly protested unto your fathers in the day that I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, even unto this day, rising early and protesting, saying, Obey my voice.
Mic 7:3
That they may do evil with both hands earnestly, the prince asketh, and the judge asketh for a reward; and the great man, he uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up.
corruption_summary: Earnestness treated as the enemy of charity, so that any warmth in defending doctrine is read as harshness — while Micah 7:3 shows the world losing none of its own earnestness at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Jude 1:3 commands a warmth about doctrine that a temperate age finds embarrassing. The Greek is epagonizomai — to agonize over, to contend as in a contest — and the object is the faith once delivered, a fixed deposit rather than an evolving consensus. A church that has learned to regard all doctrinal earnestness as a personality defect has disarmed itself by etiquette. Meanwhile Micah 7:3 notes that men lose no earnestness whatever when doing evil: they do it with both hands, and the zeal is all on one side.

But earnestness is not the same as heat, and Jeremiah 31:20 guards the difference better than any warning could. God's earnestness there is a father's aching memory of a son he has had to speak against — my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him. That is the temperature Jude's command is to be obeyed at. Contending for the faith without that ache produces a combatant; the ache without the contending produces a sentimentalist. Scripture requires both in the same man.
roots_summary: Hebrew doubled verb forms (the infinitive absolute) rendered earnestly — protesting I protested, remembering I remember; Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; ektenos (G1619), stretched out, intently.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute — the doubled verb of emphasis; I earnestly protested in Jer 11:7 is literally protesting I protested.
Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly, agonize over; used once, of the faith once delivered (Jud 1:3).
Greek ektenesteron (G1617) — more intensely, stretched further; used of the Lord's prayer in the agony (Luk 22:44).
usage: “Earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered” — a fixed deposit, contended for.
“I do earnestly remember him still” — the temperature at which the contending is to be done.
“Do evil with both hands earnestly” — the world has lost none of its zeal.
